Pro/Guides/Podcast studio

Guide · podcast and radio · 7 steps

How to build a podcast studio. Sound like radio, look like TV.

Seven steps, in the order the decisions depend on each other: the room first, then the voices, then the picture. Every step names gear from live i9Store listings with its listed price, and the end of the guide has three example budgets.

Step 01

Choose the quietest room, not the biggest.

Sound reflects off hard, parallel surfaces and comes back into the mics as echo. A furnished room with a rug, curtains, a sofa and full bookshelves sounds better than an empty one twice its size.

  • Seat the hosts facing each other across a table, away from windows, the street side and the air-conditioning vent.
  • Clap once in the empty room. A long ring means the room needs soft surfaces before it needs a better mic.
  • Leave space behind each host for a light and depth in the picture.

For size, the room planner’s podcast template starts from rooms of 4 × 3.5 m, 5.5 × 4.5 m and 7 × 6 m (planning defaults, not measured rooms).

i9Store’s catalog has no acoustic panels. If the room still rings after furnishing it, treat the walls beside and behind the hosts with panels from a local supplier.

Step 02

One mic per voice, close to the mouth.

Each voice gets its own mic, a hand’s width from the mouth, so the voice is much louder than the room. That is what makes a small room work. Buy the same model for every host so the voices match.

Kits that include a stand and headphones are the quickest start; a broadcast vocal mic is the step up.

Step 03

Record every mic on its own track.

A podcast recorder or a small mixer-recorder takes all the mics and records each one on its own track, so the edit can fix one voice without touching the others.

Count the voices you will have on your busiest episode, guests included, and check the number of mic inputs on the listing before you buy.

Step 04

For video, one camera per host or one wide shot.

A video podcast works with one wide camera on both hosts. One camera per host, plus the wide, lets the edit cut to whoever is speaking.

A tracking camera follows the speaker on its own. A mirrorless camera with a lens gives a softer background. A cinema camera body needs a lens bought separately. Put every camera at eye level.

Step 05

One soft key light per host.

Light each face from slightly to the side of its camera, as large and soft as the room allows. A small light behind the hosts separates them from the wall and gives the picture depth.

Switch off or cover warm room lamps that fall on faces: mixed colour is hard to fix in the edit.

Step 06

Switch, record and stream the picture.

A switcher takes the cameras and cuts between them. A plain switcher keeps one program cut; an ISO switcher also records each camera as its own file, so the edit can re-cut the episode.

Headphones on every host let each one hear the recording instead of the room, and catch a noisy cable before it ruins a take.

Step 07

Furniture that doesn’t creak.

A solid table and quiet chairs matter more than they look: every creak and tap reaches the mics. Mic arms or stands keep the mics off the table so knocks don’t travel into them.

Tripods put the cameras at eye level across the table. i9Store doesn’t sell tables or chairs.
